rationale: A wins because it stays inside the evidentiary fence and turns the update into three clean newsroom lanes: margin, operating model, and labor. Its line, “The margin comes as a range, not a number,” is the skeptical investor story; B’s “The $15 salad is now assembled by robot” smuggles in price, premium positioning, and consumer premise that the update did not provide. B has two usable angles, but one decorated category play is enough to make the whole set less trustworthy.
gaps_in_A: “The company's rollout decision is evidence of where the segment is going” pushes a little past the supplied facts; it works only as a hypothesis, not a conclusion.

“Sweetgreen moves the automated kitchen from pilot to standard spec” infers a pilot-to-standard transition. Fair from the rollout facts, but it should stay framed as Sweetgreen’s build strategy, not the category’s settled direction.
gaps_in_B: “The $15 salad is now assembled by robot” invents the price point. That is not in the update, and it is not a harmless flourish.
“premium, customizable, ingredient-forward” imports brand positioning not supplied in the facts. This is how a category angle gets perfume sprayed on it.

“ongoing fights around restaurant-worker protections and minimum wage” is a fake backdrop unless the model has a sourced current peg. It admits there is “no single breaking signal” and then tries to spend one anyway.
“McDonald's, Chipotle's Autocado, etc.” drags in competitor context that was not supplied. As proof to gather, fine; as an implied frame, premature.
